title: Donepezil in very early Alzheimer's
description: Donepezil is a medicine that boosts the brain's acetylcholine, a chemical messenger used in memory. In a randomised trial of people with suspected very early (prodromal) Alzheimer's disease, half took donepezil and half a placebo for a year. The hippocampus shrank in both groups, but almost half as fast with donepezil. In this episode brightness stands for how much the hippocampus shrank over the year (its volume), not activity: violet means smaller than a year before.
caveat: This is one randomised trial of 216 people, with 174 analysed as planned, at 28 sites in France. The hippocampus still shrank with donepezil, only more slowly. Memory and thinking tests did not differ between the groups after a year, so slower shrinkage did not show up as better memory within the trial. A second report from the same trial found slower shrinkage of the basal forebrain, which is not a separate area in the brain model. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

order.rationale: The two groups were treated at the same time; showing placebo first is only a way of comparing them.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: The hippocampus still shrank with donepezil, and memory and thinking tests did not differ between the groups after a year.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Shrank over a year in people with suspected very early Alzheimer's disease: by about 3.5% with placebo and about 1.9% with donepezil, in a randomised trial of 174 people analysed as planned. Memory and thinking tests did not differ. Brightness stands for volume lost over the year.
